title: Seven MVP traps, and the question that gets you out of them
summary: An MVP is a tool for learning, and it's easy to misuse. Seven common traps, from cutting too much to forgetting operations, and how to scope a first version that teaches.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The workshop starts with a lot of confidence. One column of sticky notes says "must have", another says "later", and a note in the corner says "MVP", as if the word alone will stop the team from building too much. By the end of the afternoon the board is still full, the launch date is still close, and nobody can say for sure what the first version is supposed to prove.

Eric Ries, who popularized the term, defined the MVP as the version of a new product that lets a team "collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort." In the same post he warns that "MVP, despite the name, is not about creating minimal products," and that its power is matched by the confusion it causes, because it's hard to do well (Ries, Minimum Viable Product: a guide). Used well, an MVP is a learning instrument. Used as a slogan, it turns into a permission slip to ship something confusing or too thin to teach anyone anything.

Here are seven traps that show up again and again, and what to do about each.

1. Cutting until it's no longer viable

Onboarding, helpful error messages, empty states, a support path, data checks: next to the main feature they all look optional, so they go first. Then real users touch the product, feel lost and leave. The team concludes "people didn't want it", when what they actually learned is that people couldn't understand it or didn't trust it.

Henrik Kniberg puts the problem neatly: "Your 'viable' is my 'horrible'." He suggests dropping the vague word and naming the stage you're aiming for. An Earliest Testable Product is the first release customers can actually do something with. An Earliest Usable Product is one early adopters will use willingly. An Earliest Lovable Product is one customers will love, tell friends about and pay for (Kniberg, Making sense of MVP). Saying which one you're building settles a lot of arguments about what's allowed to be missing.

2. Building too much before the first real signal

The opposite trap: the MVP becomes a smaller copy of the final dream. Settings, dashboards, integrations, role permissions and edge-case handling all arrive before anyone has tested the riskiest assumption. The product looks more complete, and the learning arrives late and expensive.

Kniberg's cautionary example is Lego Universe, an online multiplayer game. According to his account, about 250 people worked on it for 4 to 5 years, the reception was lukewarm, and the game shut down after 2 years. His summary: "There was no skateboard!" A polished first release can still be far too heavy.

3. Launching without a hypothesis

"Let's launch an MVP and see what happens" sounds flexible. Usually it hides questions the team should say out loud. What do we need to learn? That users have this problem? That they'll change how they work? That they'll pay? That it fits into their day? That it beats the spreadsheet or the manual process they already use? Without a hypothesis, any result can be explained away.

Marty Cagan uses the term "MVP Test" for these experiments, so that people don't confuse an experiment with a product, and he describes a real MVP as valuable, usable and feasible (Cagan, Minimum Viable Product). A one-line template helps: "We believe [these users] will [do this] because [reason]. We'll know we're right when [signal] reaches [level] by [date]."

4. Measuring activity instead of learning

Page views, sign-ups, clicks and demo requests are all useful, as long as they connect to the question you're testing. If the bet is that users will finish a painful workflow faster, completion rate and time saved matter more than visits. If the bet is willingness to pay, polite interest isn't enough. Pick the metrics before launch, while nobody is emotionally invested in protecting the idea yet.

5. Forgetting that minimal still has to run

A product can be minimal and still need support, monitoring, rollback, docs and an owner. If the MVP creates manual work for the team, that work is part of the experiment and should be counted. If every new user needs a developer to fix their data by hand, you've learned something important. Calling it temporary doesn't make it free.

6. Taking shortcuts nobody writes down

Some shortcuts are smart because they buy learning sooner. Others are just future confusion with a product label on them. Martin Fowler's technical debt quadrant draws the line: prudent, deliberate debt is when the team knows it's taking on debt and has thought about whether the payoff from releasing earlier is greater than the cost of paying it back (Fowler, TechnicalDebtQuadrant). The practical habit is to write down the shortcut, its risk and the condition for revisiting it. "We'll hardcode this integration for the ten pilot customers" is a decision. "We forgot it was hardcoded until customer eleven signed up" is an incident.

7. Spending trust you can't earn back

Minimal doesn't mean careless. If the product touches money, private data, health, someone's career, or anything with real emotional weight, the bar for viable goes up. The first version can be narrow, and it still has to be safe. Sometimes the smallest responsible test isn't production software at all: a clickable prototype, a waitlist conversation, or a concierge version where the team does the work by hand behind a simple front end.

The question to ask instead

"What can we remove?" is the question that leads into most of these traps. A better one: what's the smallest honest way to learn the thing that matters most right now? Try it this week. Before your next scoping session, write the hypothesis on one card, name the stage (testable, usable or lovable), pick the one signal that would change your plan, and list the shortcuts you're choosing on purpose. If the team agrees on that card, the first version doesn't have to impress anyone. It only has to teach you the next decision.

faqs.q: What is a minimum viable product?
faqs.a: Eric Ries defines it as the version of a new product that lets a team collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort. It's a tool for testing an important assumption with real users, and Ries stresses that it isn't about creating minimal products.

faqs.q: What are the most common MVP mistakes?
faqs.a: Cutting so much that users can't understand or trust the product, building too much before testing the riskiest assumption, launching without a clear hypothesis, measuring activity that doesn't answer the question, ignoring support and operations, taking shortcuts nobody records, and risking user trust in sensitive areas like money or private data.

faqs.q: How do I know if my MVP is too small or too big?
faqs.a: Name the stage you're aiming for. Henrik Kniberg splits it into an Earliest Testable Product (customers can do something with it), an Earliest Usable Product (early adopters use it willingly) and an Earliest Lovable Product (customers love it and will pay). If the release can't reach its stage, it's too thin. If it includes much more than the stage needs, it's too heavy.

faqs.q: Is technical debt acceptable in an MVP?
faqs.a: Some is, if it's deliberate. Martin Fowler describes prudent, deliberate debt as debt the team knows it's taking on, after weighing the payoff of an earlier release against the cost of paying it back. Write each shortcut down with its risk and the condition for revisiting it.
